steps.title: Median, quartiles and the IQR
steps.body:
From the same screen:
•  median: the middle value, with half the data on each side
•  \(Q_1\) and \(Q_3\): a quarter and three quarters of the way through the ordered data
•  \(\mathrm{IQR}=Q_3-Q_1\): the width of the box, the spread of the middle half

IB accepts the GDC’s quartiles; different hand methods can give slightly different values, so write “from GDC”.

The median and IQR are not pulled around by an extreme value; the mean and σ are. With the \(23\) in the list, \(\bar x=10\) sits above the median of \(9\).

steps.title: Outliers
steps.body:
A value is an outlier if it lies more than \(1.5\times\mathrm{IQR}\) beyond the box:
•  below \(Q_1-1.5\times\mathrm{IQR}\)
•  above \(Q_3+1.5\times\mathrm{IQR}\)

For the times: \(11.5+1.5\times4.5=18.25\), so \(23\) is an outlier; \(7-6.75=0.25\), so nothing at the low end.

On a box plot, whiskers stop at the last value inside the fences and outliers are marked with a cross or dot. Show the fence calculation; that is where the mark is.
steps.code:
upper fence: \(Q_3+1.5\times\mathrm{IQR}=11.5+6.75=18.25\)
\(23>18.25\), so \(23\) is an outlier

nspire.body:
Do not type \(0\) five times and \(1\) eight times. Use two lists:
•  the values \(x\) in one list
•  the frequencies \(f\) in a second list, and tell 1-Var Stats that it is the frequency list

The calculator then treats each value as if it appeared \(f\) times: \(n=\Sigma f=25\), and \(\bar x=\dfrac{\Sigma fx}{\Sigma f}\).

On the Nspire, put the values in one column (say x) and the frequencies in another (say f), then set Frequency List: f in the One-Variable Statistics dialog.

steps.title: Scaling and shifting every value
steps.body:
If every value is changed to \(y=ax+b\):
•  the mean follows the same rule: \(\bar y=a\bar x+b\)
•  so do the median and the quartiles
•  the spread is only affected by \(a\): \(\sigma_y=|a|\,\sigma_x\) and \(\mathrm{IQR}_y=|a|\,\mathrm{IQR}_x\)

Adding or subtracting a constant slides the whole data set along; the spread does not change. Multiplying stretches it.
steps.code:
times in seconds: \(y=60x\)
\(\bar y=60\times10=600\), \(\sigma_y=60\times4.71=283\)
then \(y-30\): mean \(570\), σ still \(283\)

parts: Each time is multiplied by \(60\) and then \(30\) is subtracted. Which of these changes σ?
✓ Subtracting \(30\) slides everything; the spread is unchanged.
✗ Subtracting a constant moves every value by the same amount, so the spread does not change. Only the \(\times60\) affects σ.

steps.ok: ✓ \(282\) s. The \(-30\) made no difference to σ; the mean would be \(60\times10-30=570\).
wrongs: \(252\) subtracted \(30\) from σ as well. A shift does not change the spread.
\(570\) is the new mean, not σ.
That is the old σ. Multiplying every value by \(60\) multiplies σ by \(60\).

questions.stem:
The times, in minutes, taken by \(10\) students to complete a puzzle are:
\(12,\ 15,\ 15,\ 17,\ 18,\ 20,\ 22,\ 25,\ 27,\ 34\)

parts.label: (a)
parts.text: Find the mean and the standard deviation of the times.
parts.figCap: The 10 times on a number line; the mean is the balance point.
wrongs: \(6.65\) is sx, the sample standard deviation. IB uses σx \(=6.31\).
\(19\) is the median, not the mean.

parts.label: (b)
parts.text: Find the median and the interquartile range.
parts.figCap: Box from Q₁ = 15 to Q₃ = 25, median line at 19.
wrongs: \(20\) is the 6th value; with \(10\) values the median is the mean of the 5th and 6th: \(19\).
\(22\) is the range of the middle values read off wrongly; \(Q_3-Q_1=25-15=10\).
That is the mean.

parts.label: (c)
parts.figCap: Upper fence Q₃ + 1.5 × IQR = 40; 34 is below it, so not an outlier.
parts.note: R1 is a reasoning mark: the conclusion must be stated with the comparison. Enter the fence value; the conclusion is in the mark scheme.
wrongs: \(35\) is \(Q_3+\mathrm{IQR}\); the rule uses \(1.5\times\mathrm{IQR}\).
That is the data value; the question wants the fence to compare it with.
\(0\) is the lower fence, \(15-15\); the question is about the top end.

questions.stem:
The number of goals scored by a football team in each of its matches last season is shown in the table.
\(\begin{array}{c|cccccc} \text{goals } x & 0 & 1 & 2 & 3 & 4 & 5 \\ \hline \text{frequency} & 4 & 9 & 11 & 8 & 5 & 3 \end{array}\)

parts.label: (a)
parts.text: Write down the number of matches played.
wrongs: \(15\) is \(0+1+\cdots+5\), the sum of the scores; add the frequencies.
\(6\) is the number of rows.

parts.label: (b)
parts.text: Find the mean number of goals per match.
ms: \(\dfrac{\Sigma fx}{\Sigma f}=\dfrac{90}{40}\), or 1-Var Stats with the frequency list
wrongs: \(2.5\) is the mean of \(0\) to \(5\) with the frequencies ignored. Set the frequency list.
\(6.67\) is the mean of the frequencies: lists swapped.

parts.label: (c)
parts.text: Find the standard deviation of the number of goals.
parts.figCap: Most matches lie within one σ (≈1.4 goals) of the mean 2.25.
ms: 1-Var Stats with the frequency list; \(n=40\) checked
wrongs: \(1.94\) is the variance; square-root it.

parts.label: (d)
parts.text: For a cup competition, each match score is increased by \(2\) bonus goals. Write down the mean and the standard deviation of the new scores.
parts.figCap: Adding 2 slides every bar along; the shape (and σ) does not change.
ms: adding a constant shifts the data but does not change the spread
wrongs: Adding \(2\) does not change σ: the spread stays \(1.39\).
The mean moves up by \(2\): \(4.25\).
\(4.5\) is \(2.25\times2\); the scores are increased by \(2\), not doubled.

questions.stem:
The masses, \(m\) kg, of \(50\) parcels are grouped as shown.
\(\begin{array}{c|ccccc} \text{mass (kg)} & 30\le m<40 & 40\le m<50 & 50\le m<60 & 60\le m<70 & 70\le m<80 \\ \hline \text{frequency} & 5 & 12 & 18 & 9 & 6 \end{array}\)

parts.label: (a)
parts.bad: The modal class is the class with the highest frequency: \(50\le m<60\) (frequency \(18\)). The frequency itself is not the class.
parts.figCap: Classes drawn at their midpoints; the tallest bar is 50 ≤ m < 60.

parts.label: (b)
parts.text: Calculate an estimate of the mean mass.
parts.figCap: Each class represented by its midpoint: 35, 45, 55, 65, 75.
ms: \(\dfrac{\Sigma fx}{50}\), or 1-Var Stats with midpoints and the frequency list
wrongs: \(49.8\) used the lower bounds; use the midpoints.
\(59.8\) used the upper bounds.
\(55\) is the mean of the midpoints with the frequencies ignored.

parts.label: (c)
parts.text: Calculate an estimate of the standard deviation.
parts.figCap: σ ≈ 11.4 kg from the same midpoint data.
wrongs: \(130\) is the variance.

parts.label: (d)
parts.text: Find the percentage of parcels with a mass of at least \(60\) kg.
parts.figCap: The last two classes: 15 of the 50 parcels.
wrongs: \(15\) is the number of parcels; the question asks for a percentage of \(50\).
\(12\%\) is \(6/50\): “at least \(60\)” includes the \(60\)–\(70\) class as well.
As a percentage: \(30\).
